column2: With mango juice from this one should make good pills; placed in the mouth, those fragrant ones destroy mouth diseases.
Areca nut well washed with water of the five leaves, perfumed with the pill substances according to ability, is a mouth-perfume.
The pungent fruit and the tooth-stick perfumed in cow-urine for three days, made like areca, Rama, make a sweet scent in the mouth.
Bark and pathya equal, with bamboo, joined with half a portion of camphor — a charming mouth-perfume like betel appears.
Thus the king should always guard women; he should never trust them, especially the mother of his son;
he should not sleep in the women's house at night; trust there would be artificial.
He should have him taught the crafts by trustworthy persons who speak falsely pleasant; under pretext of guarding the body he should appoint guards to him.
One should not allow his company with the angry, greedy or insulted; if instilling virtues is impossible, one should bind him by gentle means.
One trained should be appointed to all offices. The king should avoid hunting, drinking, dice, which destroy the kingdom;
daytime sleep, aimless wandering, harsh speech; one should give up censure, harshness of punishment and corruption of wealth.
Destruction of mines, wrong treatment of forts and the like, is said to be corruption of wealth, and dispersal;
a gift at wrong place and time, a gift to an unfit person, are said to be corruption of wealth, and promoting bad deeds.
One should avoid desire, anger, pride, conceit, greed and arrogance. Then, having conquered servants, one should conquer townspeople and country folk;
he should conquer outer enemies afterward; and outer enemies are of three kinds: as before, the gurus, the kinsmen, the next artificial.
The ancestral friend, the neighbor, the enemy's, and the artificial, O great one, friends are said to be of three kinds.
The lord, minister, country, fort, army, treasury and ally, knower of dharma — the kingdom is called seven-limbed.
The root is the lord; he is to be protected, therefore the kingdom especially. One should kill one who betrays a limb of the kingdom; in time one should be sharp or mild.
Thus for the king both worlds; one should avoid jesting with servants. Servants here disrespect a king who tells pleasing tales;
for winning over people he should show feigned weakness; he should speak with a smile first and please the people.
A king who is slow in action surely loses his works; but in passion, arrogance, pride, treachery and sinful work,
and in saying what is unpleasant, slowness is praised. The king should be one whose counsel sleeps; calamities do not come from guarded counsel;
for the work done is known, not the begun; his kingdom is known thereby. By appearances, hints, gait, gesture and speech,
and by changes in the eyes and face, what is within is grasped. One should not deliberate counsel alone; the king not with many;
he may consult many at will; the king should take counsel separately with each. A minister should not disclose even the counsel of ministers;
trust in someone or other always arises in men here; and the decision in counsel should be made by one wise man.
A king perishes by lack of discipline and obtains kingdom by discipline. From the three-Veda scholars he should learn the triple Veda and the eternal science of punishment,
logic, the science of wealth and the beginnings of livelihood from the people. One who has conquered the senses can keep subjects in control.
The gods and all Brahmins are to be honored, and gifts should be given to them. A gift to a Brahmin is this imperishable treasure that no one destroys.
Not turning back in battles, protecting subjects, and gifts to Brahmins are the king's highest good.
He should arrange security and livelihood for the wretched, orphans, old, widows and women;
the order of castes and stages should be maintained; ascetics should be honored; one should not trust everywhere, but should trust ascetics.
One should also make another trust by a true reason. He should think of his aim like a heron, strive like a lion,
plunder like a wolf, spring away like a hare; the king should be a hard striker like a boar,
a painter like a peacock, firmly devoted like a horse; and sweet-spoken like a cuckoo, the king should be.
Always suspicious like a crow, he should live in an unknown dwelling; he should not touch food or bed untested before;
he should not go to an unknown woman nor board an unknown boat. One who ruins the nation falls from kingdom's purpose and from life.
As a nourished calf, grown strong, becomes fit for work, so the nation, great one, nourished, becomes able to bear work.
All this action depends on arrangement, fate and human effort; of these fate is inconceivable, effort contains action.
The prosperity of the king's kingdom and earth arises from the people's affection.
Those who hate each other, are angry, afraid or insulted — among them one should apply division, one should show great fear;
one should show his own people hope; by whatever fault they fear, by that very fault the enemies are to be divided; the divider of kin is to be guarded.
The ally's treasury is external; ministers, sons and the rest are internal. Pacifying the inner treasury, he would conquer the enemy's.
Gift is the best of means; by gift one shares both worlds. There is none who does not come under control by gift;
only the giver can divide the combined enemies. One should accomplish the three-unattainable by punishment and by what is done;
all rests on punishment; wrongly applied punishment destroys. Punishing the unpunishable he perishes, and the king not punishing the punishable.
Gods, demons, serpents, men, Siddhas, beings and birds would overstep their limits if punishment were not maintained.
Since it tames the untamed and punishes the unpunishable, from taming and from punishing the wise know it as danda.
Hard to look upon through splendor like the sun, the king; then he should go to the people's favor by sight like the moon;
he pervades the world by spies, so the king is the wind; by punishing faults the king is the lord Vaivasvata (Yama);
when he burns the evil-minded he is fire; when he gives gifts to the twice-born he is the lord of wealth;
by raining streams of wealth he is remembered among gods as Varuna; bearing the worlds with forbearance the king is the earth-king;
because he protects with energy, counsel, power and the rest, therefore he is Hari.
Of cloth and the like, knower of dharma, so dharma is not diminished. One who has a deposit killed and one who asks without having deposited,
both are to be punished like thieves or fined double. A man who through ignorance sells another's goods
is blameless; but knowingly he deserves thief's punishment. One who takes the price for a craft and does not deliver is punishable;
the king should fine one who promises and does not give a suvarna. One who takes wages and does not do the work: eight krishnalas is the fine;
one who dismisses a servant out of time is fined the same amount. If one regrets having bought or sold anything here,
within ten days the owner should give back and take it; after ten days one neither takes nor makes to give.
One who takes and gives back is fined six hundred by the king. One who here betroths a maiden without disclosing the groom's faults,
she, though given, is not given; the king should fine him two hundred. One who having given a maiden to another gives her again,
the king should impose on him the highest fine. Merit joined with truthful speech and word is without doubt.
A greedy seller elsewhere deserves a six-hundred fine. A herdsman who takes food and wages and does not tend the cow
is fined a hundred by the king, or a suvarna, if unguarded. A hundred bows is the surrounding circumference of a village all around;
twice or thrice for a town. One should make a fence there that a camel cannot see over;
where grain is unfenced and damaged there is no fine. One who seizes a house, tank, garden or field by threat
is to be fined five hundred; through ignorance, two hundred. All breakers of boundaries are to be fined, the first-degree offence.
A Kshatriya who abuses a Brahmin deserves a hundred fine; a Vaishya two hundred, Rama; a Shudra deserves death.
A Brahmin who accuses a Kshatriya is fined fifty; for a Vaishya half of fifty; for a Shudra twelve is the fine.
A Vaishya gets the Kshatriya's offence as before; a Shudra who abuses a Kshatriya gets his tongue cut.
A Shudra giving dharma instruction to Brahmins is liable to punishment; one who falsifies learning, country and the like should be fined double.
The highest offence is his who casts the worthy down with sins. What I said through heedlessness and the like deserves half the fine by affection.
One who curses mother, father, elder brother, brother, father-in-law or teacher is fined a hundred, and one who does not yield the way to a teacher;
with whatever limb a low-caste man offends a twice-born, that very limb should be cut off at once without deliberation.
For spitting from arrogance the king should cut both lips; for urinating at him the organ; for breaking wind the anus;
for a low man seated on a high seat, cutting below; whoever injures a limb, that limb of his should be cut.
